reader.summary: This week was dominated by a sharp deterioration in US-Ukraine relations after President Trump waived new Russia sanctions under the Graham Act, citing national interest, just days after signing them into law. Zelenskyy called the move wrong and accused the US of helping Russia, while Moscow hailed it as historic. Congress expressed outrage but had no quick legislative counter. The timing ahead of midterms intensified partisan fights, with Democrats using the Iran war and the sanctions waiver as campaign themes. Inside the White House, press secretary Katie Zacharia was fired after just five days amid criticism over her legal credentials, adding to a pattern of turmoil. Trump also threatened California officials with imprisonment over mail-ballot rules and rallied in Georgia and Pennsylvania as Republican midterm prospects dimmed. No Kings rallies drew voters nationwide to cast early ballots. The US budget deficit ballooned to nearly two trillion dollars, the largest in five years, while interest costs hit a record one trillion. Markets were battered by a tech-sector sell-off and credit fears, with bank stocks posting their worst weekly losing streak since 2008. A school shooting in Oregon left four dead, and US-Iran tensions over the Strait of Hormuz escalated with both sides claiming control of the waterway.

display.eli5:
The US is in a real fight with Ukraine right now. President Trump signed new sanctions against Russia into law, then immediately put them on hold, saying it was in the national interest. Ukraine's leader called the move wrong, and members of Congress are furious. This is the Russia sanctions waiver story that is dominating the news this week.

Meanwhile, the US and Iran are still trading punches around a narrow stretch of sea called the Strait of Hormuz, where oil ships pass. Both sides say they control the waterway, and both have hit ships. This is the US-Iran confrontation that could get worse at any moment.

Next week, you will probably see Congress hold a big hearing about the sanctions, and both the US and Iran hit each other again in the Gulf. The midterm elections are also getting really hot, with Trump jumping into races he likes and anti-Trump groups holding big rallies to get people to vote early.

A surprise would be if the US and Iran escalate into a much bigger military clash, like a major strike on an Iranian base, which would force Congress to vote on whether the US is officially at war. That would shake up everything just before the elections.

wind.systematic_error: Both forecasters were too eager to predict concrete US military or diplomatic actions from the Iran situation. They saw escalating rhetoric and assumed strikes would materialize (Q2), a trust-building framework would be announced (Q1), Europe would be pressed for diesel (Q5), and Trump would declare near-victory (Q8). In reality, the headlines show the US still in a consideration-and-threat phase, acting unilaterally through a Russia deal and its own strategic reserve, and using broad language about control rather than specific victory declarations. The forecasters confused planning language with execution and assumed multilateral coordination where the evidence shows bilateral or unilateral moves.
wind.correction_hint: When US headlines say a strike is 'being considered' or 'may need to happen,' treat it as not yet done and mark the question NO unless a headline explicitly reports the strike occurring. Distinguish between the US acting through its own tools (SPR, Russia deals) versus pressuring allies, and between Trump saying the war will end when he wants versus declaring he is close to total victory.
